items.en: First, the bad news: Of all the rivers in the contiguous United States, only 6 percent are both in healthy condition and meaningfully safeguarded. The good news is that many more may be just one repair away from thriving.

A new map highlights where conservation money and attention would do the most good as the climate warms, researchers report September 16 in PLOS One. The effort is the most comprehensive to date, assessing the health of the lower 48 states’ rivers and streams.

“We can now point at a map for the first time and say, these are the rivers most capable of sustaining diversity of aquatic life, and this is what each one needs,” says Mary Khoury, a freshwater ecologist at The Nature Conservancy who is based in Chicago.

For decades, conservation in the United States has been organized primarily around land. Scientists know for the most part which forests are intact and who owns what. Rivers have never gotten that treatment, even as more than 150,000 dams have fragmented the country’s waterways — cutting fish off from spawning grounds and cold-water refuges — and climate change has altered the temperatures and flows these animals depend on.

The new assessment, which took four years, maps one-third of the nation’s stream distances. Each small watershed was rated on four measures: how connected its river network is, meaning whether animals including fish and mussels can freely travel along it; the condition of its floodplain and water quality; how much water it has; and how much its flows have been altered. Those ratings were laid over 91 existing assessments of where freshwater life is concentrated. Dozens of scientists and partners from 44 states adjusted the measures for river systems in regions as different as the humid East, the arid Great Plains and the deserts of the Southwest.

A four-year assessment graded every river and stream in the lower 48 for its ability to sustain aquatic life in a warming climate. The healthiest ones cluster along the Pacific Coast, in the northern Rockies and across the Southeast. The most vulnerable sit in the Southwest deserts, the Great Plains and southern New England.

Rivers doing well on all four criteria — more than half of the mapped stream distances — came out as resilient. The rest score near average, and were classed as restorable, still functional but held back by a problem, such as runoff from a farm or an obstructing dam, that one intervention could solve.

Together the two categories form what the authors call a freshwater resilient and connected network, a shopping list of what the country would need to look after to keep its freshwater life going. “A resilient system is one that gives species options and environments in which to adapt,” Khoury says.

Dams leave the clearest mark on the country’s rivers, carving them into more than 9,000 separate pieces. The study maps where reconnecting rivers would pay off most. Among the long unbroken stretches within the resilient system are Oregon and California’s Klamath River, whose lower dams came out in the largest removal project in U.S. history, and the Delaware River, which runs free of barriers along its main stem from New York’s Catskill Mountains to the sea.

“I can see this being overlaid in the future, for example, with where dam licenses will expire, in order to find the most effective restoration opportunities,” says Rafael Schmitt, a hydrologist at the University of California, Santa Barbara who was not involved in the work.

Unlike on land, the study found, a river’s health says almost nothing about whether anyone is looking after it. On land, the healthiest places tend to be the protected ones. In water, however, 13 percent of the country’s stream distances are in good shape with no real safeguards, roughly twice the 6 percent that is both healthy and protected.

The unprotected healthy rivers are the ones most at risk of slipping, because nothing keeps them in that condition. Locking in protection is harder for a river than for a forest. A designated preserve can hold a kilometer of stream while the water arriving in it may drain 100 kilometers of farm fields, dams and subdivisions. “It matters what’s going on upstream of that protected area,” Khoury says.

What if you lost your voice? Today, AI can re-create it, and brain implants can turn thoughts into speech. This season of The Deep End follows people living through these vocal transformations — and asks what these remarkable technologies can teach us about why our voices matter in the first place. Episodes will drop Tuesdays, starting Oct. 6.
Laura Sanders: One of today’s most powerful pieces of technology is something we’ve had all along…
Laura: The human voice. If you’ve ever saved and replayed a voicemail, or called someone just to hear their voice…
Female voice: Hey dude, I’m just calling to say hi and chitchat.
Laura: Then you know that voices can connect, soothe, inspire, scare, seduce and make us laugh until we cry.
Laura: Our voices make us who we are, but what happens when they are lost?
MA Fernandez: I still remember the first time that I heard the first little crack in his voice that let me know something’s changing.

Laura: Welcome to The Deep End, a podcast about our brains and ourselves. I’m Laura Sanders, a reporter with Science News. And on this season, called Talk to Me, we dive into the latest scientific research to answer the question, “What happens when a voice is lost? And can it be found again?”
Jules Rodriguez: When I first heard my cloned voice, it felt like I reappeared.
Laura: Across six episodes, you’ll hear a chorus of voices like Casey, who has a brain implant that can pull words from his thoughts.

Casey Harrell: The ability to scream when you are running and want to get out some stress. The ability to say sweet nothings into your partner’s ear. These are the things that life is all about. And when you are robbed of those times, you want them back at all costs.
Laura: You’ll hear from Jules, who performs live comedy sets with a voice cloned through artificial intelligence.
Jules: Do I want to be right, or do I want to eat tonight. [laughter]
Laura: And you’ll hear from Patrick, a musician who sings with a synthetic voice.
Patrick: (Singing) Then played the rocky road, with a fire and a glow.

Laura: Synthetic voice clones, brain implants and even AI voices that can speak at their own funerals, like it or not, the story of the human voice is changing. Let’s talk about it. Listen to The Deep End: Talk to Me wherever you get your podcasts.

Before the sun fully formed, tiny bits of rock were already recording the magnetic forces present in the very early solar system. More than 4.5 billion years later, scientists have learned how to read that record.

The ancient rocks suggest that the turbulent cloud of gas and dust that gave rise to our solar system was shot through a powerful magnetic field. That field may have helped feed the growing sun, researchers report August 24 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The findings suggest gravity may not have acted alone to build our solar system or the countless other planetary systems in the Milky Way and beyond.

That ancient record is preserved in meteorites — time capsules of material that formed long ago. In particular, rocks that contain specific speckly mineral inclusions really turn back the clock. These inclusions solidified more than 4.5 billion years ago, before the sun and planets, says Cauê Borlina, a planetary scientist at Purdue University in West Lafayette, Ind. “They’re forming before everything else.”

Scientists have long debated whether the gas that makes up the sun was shepherded into place mainly by gravity or by a magnetic field. Previous studies suggest the presence of a solar system –wide magnetic field after the sun formed. What’s been much harder to determine is whether that field was already present during the sun’s earliest stages of formation, Borlina says.

He and his colleagues analyzed a meteorite that fell to Earth in 2008. The team focused on five inclusions containing iron, an element whose electrons readily rearrange to record magnetic fields. Using sensitive magnetometers, the researchers measured magnetic fields of a few gauss, a common unit of magnetism. That’s several times stronger than Earth’s current magnetic field.

Simulations of planetary system formation predict that stronger magnetic fields will transport more gas toward the nascent star, Borlina says. During the sun’s earliest, or Class 0, phase some models suggest it could have gobbled up more than 300 Earth masses of gas each year. The newly measured field is strong enough that magnetism could have contributed substantially to that feeding frenzy. “You can’t ignore the contribution of magnetism,” Borlina says.

These results provide an important look at the solar system’s very beginnings, says Indrani Das, a theoretical astrophysicist at the Academia Sinica Institute of Astronomy and Astrophysics in Taipei, Taiwan. “This is one of the first measurements that has been done of the Class 0 phase.”
Still, these findings need to be bolstered with measurements from other meteorites, Das says. “We need a bigger sample size.”
A new NASA directive seeks to loosen “planetary protection” rules meant to avoid the contamination other worlds with microbial life from Earth.

The policy shift arrived via a message to NASA personnel that was obtained and shared yesterday by the independent watchdog sites NASA Watch and Astrobiology.com. In it, NASA administrator Jared Isaacman writes that procedures for avoiding contamination “must reflect our current scientific knowledge” and argues that this knowledge has shifted since the current rules were established decades ago.

The directive “ensures we can use our incredible data to lower costs on our missions,” says Nicky Fox, associate administrator of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate. “This process will also help increase commercial capabilities—getting more missions into space by streamlining space exploration.”

In 1964 members of the International Council for Science’s Committee on Space Research (COSPAR), led by the United Nations–affiliated International Council of Scientific Unions (now the International Science Council), feared that the breakneck pace of the space race could lead to spacecraft accidentally contaminating alien worlds with microbial life from Earth. If those interplanetary hitchhikers were sufficiently resilient and numerous to form self-sustaining populations on Mars or other planets, they could forever alter those otherwise-pristine environments and sabotage all future efforts to discover true alien life there. So COSPAR issued a resolution that any mission to another potentially habitable or inhabited world must demonstrate a less than one-in-10,000 chance of exposing such places to terrestrial life capable of interplanetary colonization.

The new directive notes that COSPAR subsequently tightened those rules to account for the flurry of Mars-bound missions, some carrying human crews, that were widely expected to launch in the intervening decades. Codified in 1969, those more stringent and costly restrictions have guided—and greatly limited, some critics say—Mars exploration ever since. But “human exploration did not progress as quickly as all believed,” Isaacman’s message reads, while technology for sterilizing spacecraft has improved markedly. “Our long-standing policies were designed in a different era,” he writes.

Now, the message states, NASA’s rules will immediately be restored to the looser 1964 restriction of less than a one-in-10,000 chance of biocontamination for each Mars-bound mission. And in the meantime, NASA officials will perform a rapid-fire “modernization assessment” of the current science and technology concerning contamination risk, with a December 2026 deadline for delivering recommendations to lower that threshold even further.

Cassie Conley, NASA’s former (and longest-serving) planetary protection officer, is critical of the change. Given how little we still know about possible life on Mars, she says, relaxing biological contamination constraints now is “idiocy.”

“I used to point out that planetary protection was probably the first time in history that humans had grown up enough, together as a global species, to decide not to do irreversible and possibly stupid things before we understood the consequences,” she says. “Too bad it didn’t last.”

In a statement shared with Scientific American, NASA clarified that, with the new directive, the agency isn’t weakening existing planetary protection protocols so much as updating them. “This directive moves NASA toward a quantitative, performance-based approach that measures actual contamination risk and applies protections accordingly,” the statement said. Additionally, missions looking for past or present life will “continue to carry requirements appropriate to protecting those investigations.”

Such cautions are crucial, experts say, especially because NASA’s Perseverance rover on Mars has uncovered tantalizing hints of possible ancient biosignatures in some of the rocks it has studied. Samples from those rocks are now in limbo, awaiting an as-yet-unclear ride back to Earth for further analysis.

“We are actively seeking to learn if the organics we have found on Mars are biological in origin,” says Linday Hays, NASA’s senior scientist for Mars exploration. This policy change will not threaten that goal, she says, but “will allow us to bring decades of science from our Mars exploration to help make our processes more straightforward for robotic and, in the future, human exploration of the Red Planet.”
